wbs.title: Work breakdown structure: island music festival
wbs.what: Decomposition in action — one level of deliverables, then sub-tasks. The shape examiners expect.
wbs.caption: Festival WBS (adapted from Worksheet 1's island music-festival brief). Every box is ownable work; numbering feeds the dependency column.
wbs.alt: Tree diagram: music festival splits into transport, catering, stage, bookings, safety, each with sub-tasks.

wbs.title: Decomposition: useful vs useless
wbs.what: Same project, two breakdowns — only one can be estimated or scheduled.
wbs.caption: Good boxes are ownable, estimable tasks; bad boxes are vague phases or milestones masquerading as work.
wbs.alt: Side-by-side comparison of a good and bad work breakdown.

left.title: ✓ Useful breakdown
points: '1.1 Ferry timetable' — one owner, days of work

right.title: ✗ Useless breakdown
points: 'Do transport stuff' — who owns it? how long?
'Track tested' is a milestone, not a task
Poker bids of ∞ or ? signal: split this box

wbs.why: The exam never asks you to admire a WBS — it asks you to estimate, order and schedule from one. Only the left column supports that.

hotspots.title: Timing box
hotspots.text: Each node carries ES · EF on top, LS · LF below. Durations stay on the node — AOA puts them on arrows instead.

hotspots.title: Slack 4 (green)
hotspots.text: B can slip 4 weeks without moving the deadline. Borrow resources here first.

hotspots.title: Critical chain ★
hotspots.text: Zero-slack nodes (A → C → …) form the critical path. Their sum must equal the project duration.

activity-graphs.title: Timing analysis in four passes
activity-graphs.what: The exact algorithm behind every 2022 Q1.2(b)-style question.
activity-graphs.caption: Forward for earliest, backward for latest, subtract for slack, chain the zeros.
activity-graphs.alt: Four-step procedure: forward pass, backward pass, slack, critical path.

steps.title: Forward pass → earliest
steps.text: Start at day 0. ES = max(EF of predecessors); EF = ES + duration. Project duration = max EF.

steps.title: Backward pass → latest
steps.text: End activities take LF = duration. LF = min(LS of successors); LS = LF − duration. Work backwards.

steps.title: Subtract → slack
steps.text: Slack = LS − ES (= LF − EF). Shared along paths — spending it here removes it downstream.

steps.title: Chain the zeros → critical path
steps.text: Join zero-slack activities; verify their durations sum exactly to the project duration. If not, recheck successors.

critical-path.title: 2022 Project A: the network that decides the deadline
critical-path.what: Trace the gold chain — the only sequence with zero slack, totalling exactly 25 weeks.
critical-path.caption: Critical path A → D → F → G → H = 3+10+3+5+4 = 25 weeks = project duration ✓. Slack lives on B (4), C (4), E (3).
critical-path.alt: Project A network with critical path highlighted and slack annotated.

gantt-charts.title: From network to calendar: a Gantt sketch
gantt-charts.what: Bars place each activity at its ES; gold bars are the deadline-drivers.
gantt-charts.caption: Same mini-network as the AON figure. B's bar floats with 4 weeks of slack; the gold chain admits no float.
gantt-charts.alt: Gantt chart with critical activities highlighted.

chart.note: Bars start at earliest-start times from the forward pass.

lifecycle-models.title: Three answers to 'how do we organise this?'
lifecycle-models.what: Cost of change grows left-to-right; feedback arrives earlier as you move down the list.
lifecycle-models.caption: Waterfall sequences phases; iterative waterfall adds feedback loops; spiral curls around risk; prototypes answer questions cheaply first.
lifecycle-models.alt: Timeline of lifecycle models with feedback characteristics.

milestones.label: Phases in order
milestones.text: Requirements → design → code → test. Cheap when stable; late change cascades expensively.

milestones.label: Iterative waterfall
milestones.text: Same phases, but later stages can send work back. The 2022 Q1.1 answer: order + loops + cost-of-change.

milestones.label: Spiral
milestones.text: Loop: set objectives → resolve risks → develop → plan next cycle. For risky, large, novel systems.

milestones.label: Prototyping
milestones.text: Quick, possibly throwaway build to answer one question (UI? feasibility?) before committing.

lifecycle-models.title: Waterfall vs spiral: when each wins
lifecycle-models.what: Match the model to the uncertainty, not to fashion.
lifecycle-models.caption: Stable requirements → waterfall's cheap sequence. High risk → spiral's explicit risk cycles.
lifecycle-models.alt: Comparison of waterfall and spiral models.

left.title: Iterative waterfall
points: Phases run in order with limited feedback

right.title: Spiral
points: Each cycle attacks the biggest remaining risk
Cost: overhead of repeated planning cycles

lifecycle-models.why: 2022 Q1.1 rewards: phase order + feedback loops + step-back example + cost-of-change consequence.

estimation-planning-poker.alt: Bar chart of two poker rounds showing converging estimates.

scrum-framework.title: Scrum's three accountabilities
scrum-framework.what: One backlog owner, one building team, one process guardian — and a team that manages itself.
scrum-framework.caption: Product Owner owns priorities; Developers own the increment; Scrum Master owns process health. Change enters via the backlog, never mid-sprint.
scrum-framework.alt: Hub diagram of Scrum roles and their responsibilities.

lines: Mid-project change → PO → backlog → future sprint

scrum-events-backlogs.title: Walking one sprint, event by event
scrum-events-backlogs.what: Four events, four purposes — inspect the product, then inspect the process.
scrum-events-backlogs.caption: Planning commits, dailies steer, review demos to stakeholders, retrospective improves the team itself.

steps.title: 1 · Sprint planning (start)
steps.text: PO presents priorities; Developers select items and plan delivery. Output: Sprint Goal + Sprint Backlog commitment.

steps.title: 2 · Daily stand-ups
steps.text: ~15 min: what was done, what is next, blockers. Developers sync; the plan adapts.

steps.title: 3 · Sprint review (end)
steps.text: Demo the working increment to stakeholders; adapt the Product Backlog. Inspects the PRODUCT.

steps.title: 4 · Retrospective (after review)
steps.text: Team reflects on its own process and agrees improvements. Inspects the PROCESS. Then the next sprint begins.

burn-up-charts.title: Burn-up simulator: plan vs reality
burn-up-charts.what: Drag the sliders — see how pace and scope shocks move the lines examiners ask you to read.
burn-up-charts.caption: Planned = total ÷ duration × t. Actual = earned value (estimates of finished tasks). Scope line rises when work is added mid-flight. Illustrative simulator — plug in your own WBS numbers.
burn-up-charts.alt: Interactive burn-up chart with adjustable pace and scope.

chart.note: Illustrative simulation for intuition, not course data. Exam arithmetic uses the SUMIF method from Worksheet 2.

hotspots.title: Pile-up = bottleneck
hotspots.text: Review is full (3/3) while Coding has one card: work cannot be pulled forward. Rebalance the team toward reviewing.

hotspots.title: Done means accepted
hotspots.text: A card here was merged AND accepted. Defects found later move the card back to an active column — within WIP.

code-review.title: The review loop inside the workflow
code-review.what: Review sits after coding, before merge — and re-review closes the loop regressions open.
code-review.caption: Lightweight peer review fits agile pace; formal inspection is reserved for critical code.
code-review.alt: Step sequence of code review workflow.

steps.title: 1 · Submit
steps.text: Author finishes code + tests; the Kanban card enters Review. Checklist attached (5–8 items, tuned to reviewer experience).

steps.title: 2 · Inspect
steps.text: Reviewer reads for logic defects — the fault class testing misses. Automate style/types; spend humans on reasoning.

steps.title: 3 · Fix
steps.text: Author addresses findings. Trivial fixes applied directly; design issues discussed, not silently patched.

steps.title: 4 · Re-review + merge
steps.text: Fixed defects re-verified (regressions re-occur), then merged. Card advances to Awaiting Merge → Done.

code-review.title: Peer review vs formal inspection
code-review.what: Match review weight to code criticality — the Worksheet 2 Q4 judgement call.
code-review.caption: Fast visualisation tool → lightweight peer review + checklist. Safety-critical core → formal inspection with roles and logging.
code-review.alt: Comparison of peer review and formal inspection.

right.title: Formal inspection
points: Overkill that slows a visualisation tool

code-review.why: The exam asks 'is formal inspection suitable here?' — answer with pace-vs-criticality, then draft the checklist.
